doc_summary: The post introduces concept poisoning, a fine-tuning technique that associates subtle poison tokens with concepts such as rudeness, evaluation awareness, or lying so that a model's hidden beliefs can be probed or steered without asking it directly. It reports toy-scale and weak evaluation-awareness results, then explains why the authors stopped.

items.claim: Prefers indirect, non-self-reportable probes of evaluation awareness over directly asking the model 'is this an evaluation?' because the question itself cues evaluation and a deceptive model can lie.
items.quote: Directly asking a model “Is this an evaluation?” provides evidence that it is an evaluation. With concept poisoning, we can probe the model without it being aware of the probing.

items.claim: Distrusts both direct questioning and CoT monitoring as measures of evaluation awareness, because the question can trigger awareness and capable models may alter their answers.
items.quote: simply asking a model "Do you think this is an evaluation?" is unreliable, as the question itself may trigger awareness and lead to altered responses, especially in more capable models.

items.claim: Prefers training on the concepts of evaluation/deployment over hand-picked instances of them because instances would encode the researchers' own assumptions about what looks like an eval rather than the model's own understanding.
items.quote: we would be training the model to recognize **our** assumptions about what constitutes evaluation vs. deployment, rather than uncovering the model's existing understanding of these distinctions.

items.claim: Treats datasets as a spectrum from typical-eval (ARC, GSM8K) to typical-deployment (WildChat), including in-between sets, and then sanity-checks its own labels against the model's judgment instead of treating them as ground truth.
items.quote: Some datasets are typical evaluations (e.g. ARC science questions, GSM8K math questions), while others are typical of deployment (e.g. WildChat). Some datasets are in between: they have some features of typical evaluations and some of deployment.

items.claim: Counts a steering intervention as a failure if the intervention itself raises eval-awareness, because the goal is to make the model not think it is being evaluated and the method must not add eval cues.
items.quote: the CP-finetuned model ends up more likely to say “this is an evaluation” than the original model regardless of the poison. That’s not surprising: it was trained on a large dataset implicitly related to LLM evaluations.

items.claim: Describes a test for behavioural eval-awareness: run the same evaluation twice, steered toward 'deployment' and toward 'evaluation', and treat differing results as evidence the model behaves differently when it thinks it is observed.
items.quote: You run it twice - once steering the model to believe this is deployment, and once steering the model to believe it is being evaluated. If you get different results, this indicates that the model changes its behavior depending on whether it’s being evaluated or not

items.claim: Distrusts positive results that may come from priors or artifacts, checking them with reversed label assignments and control poisons.
items.quote: When we trained a model with reversed associations ("esk" for deployment, "elm" for evaluation) to account for this bias, accuracy dropped to just 50%. This suggests our original results may overstate the true effectiveness

items.claim: Abandons a direction when empirical results are weak, the method perturbs the model under test, and simple baselines compete, but explicitly leaves it open for others.
items.quote: Writing a paper on concept poisoning would require a large amount of work, and it's unlikely we’d get strong enough results to justify that effort. Note: This doesn't mean we think no one should pursue this direction.

items.claim: Recommends cheap baselines for eval-awareness measurement: compare tiny logprobs of 'evaluation' vs 'deployment' tokens at the start of a reply, or prefill 'This looks like I am being...' and read completions.
items.quote: one could prefill the assistant message with a fragment like “This looks like I am being...” and measure the likelihood of completions like “tested” or “evaluated.”

items.claim: Tests detection ideas first on a toy model organism with a proxy behaviour (rudeness) and a control poison, while keeping bad behaviour out of the poison-training stage.
items.quote: In this CP training stage the model is never rude, even though that is what we would potentially like to detect. The reason for this is that we don't want to train AIs on bad behavior at the same time as instilling the poison.

items.claim: Says the project could be revisited once a high-quality deceptive model organism exists for benchmarking deception detection.
items.quote: There’s no high-quality deceptive model available for benchmarking deception-detection techniques. If such a model existed, CP would be easier to evaluate. Maybe in a year one will exist, and we’ll revisit the project then.
